title: Design Hit Counter
description: Design a hit counter that counts hits received in the past 5 minutes using a sliding-window queue.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Design a hit counter that counts the number of hits received in the past 5 minutes (300 seconds). Implement the HitCounter class with two operations: hit(timestamp), which records a hit at the given timestamp, and getHits(timestamp), which returns the number of hits recorded in the inclusive time window (timestamp - 300, timestamp].

blocks.title: Constraint
blocks.text: Timestamps passed to hit and getHits are strictly non-decreasing across all calls, and time is measured in seconds. Multiple hits can arrive at the same timestamp.

blocks.caption: Hits enter a queue; stale hits are evicted before every count query.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Operations","hit(timestamp), getHits(timestamp)"],["Window","Inclusive of (timestamp - 300, timestamp], i.e. the past 300 seconds"],["Constraint","timestamp is a positive, non-decreasing sequence across calls"],["Goal","Design each operation to run efficiently (amortized O(1) or better)"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

Whenever a problem asks how many events happened in the last X time units, with new events always arriving in non-decreasing time order, that is a sliding time window over a stream. A queue is the natural structure: new hits are appended at the back, and hits that fall outside the window are removed from the front, since timestamps only increase.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: This is the same family as Number of Recent Calls (a fixed 3000ms window), but framed as a full class with hit and getHits as separate operations instead of one combined ping method.
3. Understand the Problem

Think of a turnstile counter at a subway station that only cares about entries from the last 5 minutes. Every time someone walks through, that entry is logged with its time. When asked how many people entered recently, the counter forgets any entry older than 5 minutes and reports what remains.

blocks.caption: Old entries expire out of the window; only recent ones count.

items: hit(timestamp) simply records that a hit happened at that exact time.
getHits(timestamp) must count only the hits whose recorded time satisfies t > timestamp - 300.
Since timestamps are non-decreasing, once a hit falls outside the window it can never re-enter it later, so it can be permanently discarded.

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Trace: hit(1), hit(2), hit(3), getHits(4), hit(300), getHits(300), getHits(301).

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: At getHits(301), the window start is 1, and timestamp 1 satisfies 1 <= 1, so it is evicted. Timestamps 2, 3, and 300 all satisfy t > 1, so they remain, giving a result of 3.
5. How Should We Think?
The direct approach is to store every hit and, on each getHits call, scan the entire history to count how many fall in the window. This works but repeats work on every query.

Since timestamps never decrease, hits leave the window in the same order they entered it, first in first out. A queue lets us evict expired hits from the front without ever having to look at hits still inside the window, so each hit is evicted at most once across the whole run.
6. Brute Force Solution
Store every hit timestamp in a list. On getHits, iterate through the entire list and count timestamps satisfying t > timestamp - 300.
7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time (hit)","O(1)","Just append to the list"],["Time (getHits)","O(n)","Rescans every stored hit, including ones long expired"],["Space","O(n)","Every hit is kept forever, even expired ones"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: The list only ever grows, and old hits that will never matter again are still scanned on every single getHits call. This wastes work that a queue-based eviction avoids.
8. Optimize the Solution

Use a queue (deque) to store hit timestamps in arrival order. On getHits, before counting, pop expired timestamps (those satisfying t <= timestamp - 300) off the front of the queue and discard them permanently, since they can never become valid again as timestamps only increase. The count is then simply the size of the remaining queue.

items: hit(timestamp): push timestamp to the back of the queue, O(1).
getHits(timestamp): pop from the front while the front value <= timestamp - 300, then return the queue size.
Each hit is pushed once and popped at most once across the entire sequence of calls, giving amortized O(1) per operation.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Non-decreasing timestamps plus a fixed time window is a strong signal for a queue-based sliding window.
Evicted elements never need to be revisited, which is what makes the eviction loop amortized O(1) per operation overall.
The same eviction-from-the-front pattern applies to any count events within the last X time units streaming design problem.

blocks.text: 12. Final Summary

Design Hit Counter is solved by storing hits in a queue in arrival order and lazily evicting expired hits from the front whenever getHits is called. Because timestamps never decrease, this eviction is safe, permanent, and amortized O(1) per hit, turning an O(n) per-query brute force into an efficient streaming counter.
